# Valāhaka Saṁyutta (SN 32)

**Title (Pali):** Valāhaka Saṁyutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Linked Discourses on Cloud Gods

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Valāhaka Saṁyutta* (SN 32) is the thirty-second collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, standing as the last of a group of four thematic sections (SN 29–32) that treat semi-celestial or mythological classes of beings [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003]. The samyutta focuses on the *valāhaka-kāyikā devas*—the deities of the cloud-dwelling order who govern the weather [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003; Hazra 1994]. According to the discourses, these beings are classified into five orders: cool-cloud (*sīta-valāhaka*), warm-cloud (*uṇha-valāhaka*), storm- or thunder-cloud (*abbha-valāhaka*), wind-cloud (*vāta-valāhaka*), and rain-cloud deities (*vassa-valāhaka*) [Bodhi 2003; Hazra 1994; Lim 2009]. In suttas framed as inquiries by a visiting monk at Sāvatthī, the Buddha explains that shifts in weather (such as sudden cold, heat, wind, or rainfall) occur when these devas decide to revel in their own bodily delight, causing the elements to manifest in accordance with their wish [Rhys Davids 1924; Bodhi 2003; Lim 2009]. The collection also outlines the karmic causes leading to rebirth among these cloud deities, rooted in aspiration and deeds of generosity [Bodhi 2003].

Commentarial tradition clarifies that these devas reside in space in the company of the cloud dwellers [Bodhi 2003]. While SuttaCentral treats the collection under two main sutta headings, standard printed editions expand the text into dozens of repetitive permutations based on specific gifts and aspirations [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003; Lim 2009]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus reflects this highly formulaic structure: the collection shares extensive textual passages and karmic exposition templates with its immediate predecessors, the *Nāga Saṁyutta* (SN 29), *Gandhabbakāya Saṁyutta* (SN 31), and *Supaṇṇa Saṁyutta* (SN 30), as well as discourses dealing with rebirth intentions such as the *Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta* (MN 120) and sections of AN 8 [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments identified by DharmaNexus include matches in the Chinese *Qishi jing* (T 24), the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99), and the *Ekottarikāgama* (T 125) [DharmaNexus].
